prompt.context: Your client is Hungry Hospital. It has 800 beds and is located in a metropolitan area. It supports both in-patient and out-patient care. It accepts patients regardless of their ability to pay. Last year it had revenues of $1.2 billion. Hungry Hospital is currently under budget pressures, but has received bond approval to restructure its food services division. The division provides food for all of its patients.
prompt.question: The hospital must decide whether to outsource or build the capability to provide food services in-house. How would you structure your decision?

clarifying_info.q: What do nearby hospitals do for food services?
clarifying_info.a: All nearby hospitals outsource their patient meals.

clarifying_info.q: Has any prior research been done given the bond approval?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — the bond measure approval means prior research on much of the data has already been conducted.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any specific quality or patient satisfaction concerns?
clarifying_info.a: That information has not been provided; you may consider it as part of your qualitative analysis.

framework: Define the two alternatives clearly: (1) outsource food services to a vendor, (2) build in-house capability
Conduct NPV and/or break-even analysis comparing total costs of each alternative over a relevant time horizon
Identify all cost components for each option (see cost analysis below)
Assess qualitative / non-financial considerations: quality, flexibility, public support, synergies
Review practical constraints: available space, current staff, transition complexity
Benchmark against comparable hospitals (nearby hospitals all outsource — relevant data point)
Synthesize financial and qualitative findings into a recommendation

questions.prompt: What costs are associated with the outsourcing option?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: (1) per-meal cost charged by the vendor, (2) internal staff and management needed to oversee the vendor contract. Should probe for volume assumptions (800 beds, occupancy rate, meals per patient per day).

questions.prompt: What costs are associated with building in-house capability?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify fixed/up-front costs and ongoing variable costs. Fixed: capital construction or equipment financed via bond. Variable: food ingredients, labor (kitchen staff), insurance, utilities, space/facility costs. Should consider depreciation and the cost of capital on the bond financing.

questions.prompt: How would you get the data necessary to conduct this analysis?
questions.guidance: Strong answers reference: (1) the bond measure approval implies feasibility and cost data already exist, (2) request vendor quotes for outsourcing, (3) benchmark nearby hospitals — all outsource, (4) internal data on patient census/meal volumes, (5) contractor bids for construction if building in-house.

questions.prompt: What non-financial considerations should influence the decision?
questions.guidance: Quality of patient meals and impact on patient outcomes/satisfaction; flexibility to change vendors vs. locked-in capital; public/community perception (hospital accepts all patients regardless of ability to pay — brand matters); potential synergies with existing cafeteria or staff dining operations; employee relations if existing food staff would be affected; regulatory or accreditation requirements for hospital food.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond cost-benefit analysis, what other considerations should Hungry Hospital weigh?

categories.name: Quality & Patient Outcomes
ideas: Vendor specialization may yield better nutritional standards
In-house allows tighter control over special dietary needs (allergy, religious, clinical diets)
Patient satisfaction scores tied to meal quality affect hospital ratings

categories.name: Financial & Strategic
ideas: Bond financing introduces debt service obligations regardless of option chosen
Outsourcing converts fixed costs to variable costs — better flexibility under census fluctuations
In-house investment builds a long-term asset; could serve staff and visitors as revenue stream

categories.name: Operational & Practical
ideas: Available kitchen space within the existing facility
Transition risk and timeline for either option
Vendor lock-in and contract renegotiation risk
Existing staff: layoffs vs. retraining if outsourcing

categories.name: External Benchmarking
ideas: All nearby hospitals outsource — suggests outsourcing is the industry norm
Could signal vendor market is mature and competitive, lowering outsourcing cost
May indicate regulatory or practical reasons in-house is sub-optimal at this scale

categories.name: Stakeholder & Community
ideas: Hospital accepts all patients regardless of ability to pay — community goodwill matters
Labor union considerations if hospital employees are affected
Public support for the bond was presumably contingent on responsible stewardship

recommendation: No single right answer — recommend whichever option the candidate's analysis supports, delivered confidently

If outsourcing: recommend issuing RFPs to specialized food-service vendors, structuring a performance-based contract with quality and nutritional KPIs, and using bond proceeds for transition costs and contract setup
If in-house: recommend using bond proceeds for kitchen capital build-out, hiring a nutrition director, and phasing implementation to minimize disruption
risks: Outsourcing: vendor quality drift over time, price escalation at contract renewal, loss of operational control
In-house: construction overruns, ongoing fixed cost burden if census declines, management distraction from core clinical mission
next_steps: Obtain vendor quotes and run full NPV comparison with sensitivity analysis on census volume
Assess physical space availability for in-house option
Review bond covenants for any restrictions on use of proceeds
Survey patient and staff preferences on meal quality
